title: Show HN: Kairos – Open-source risk and fraud decisioning platform
author: ayanb9440
summary: Hey HN, Ayan here from Finic. We’re launching Kairos, an open source alternative to Sift, Sardine, and other real-time fraud decisioning platforms. Kairos addresses two of the biggest problems facing traditional decisioning tools: a lack of labeled data to train on and dealing with fraudsters that are constantly changing their tactics. 1. Traditional fraud solutions use ML models such as XGBoost to detect fraud, but these models are dependent on quality labeled data which many businesses do not have. We address this by using “System One” decision models in additional to traditional models such as XGBoost and logistic regression. This allows you to incorporate plain language questions such as “Is this a throwaway email” into your decisioning, bypassing the need for large amounts of labeled data. This also allows you to capture aspects of fraud that are more unstructured, which is something that XGBoost models struggle with. 2. Fraud teams are facing off with live players that are constantly changing their behavior to bypass the detection logic they have in place. You can train a detection model or define a ruleset once, but it will become obsolete in a matter of weeks as fraudsters figure out what your detection logic is. This means that you need a team regularly training models and updating rules based on new fraud patterns. Typically this takes a large data science/ML team. Kairos addresses this by introducing an MCP server, so that your agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, etc.) can define a decision workflow, train models on your data, and pick the variant that performs best. You can self-host Kairos with Docker or use the hosted version at https://kairos.finic.ai Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50358314 Points: 25 # Comments: 2

title: Why youtube-transcript-api gets blocked on servers, and what works
author: Govind Siwakoti
summary: Originally published at https://lurkapi.com/blog/youtube-transcript-api-blocked When youtube-transcript-api works on your laptop and raises RequestBlocked on AWS, a VPS, Colab or a CI runner, your code is fine. YouTube is refusing your server’s IP: it answers requests from cloud and datacenter addresses with “Sign in to confirm you’re not a bot” instead of captions, and the library gives up in under a second. From a fresh cloud server, 1 of 10 popular videos comes back; the other nine raise RequestBlocked . Two fixes still work: send the library through rotating residential proxies, or let a hosted transcript API make the request so your server never talks to YouTube. The third fix the error message offers, cookies, is switched off in the current release. The block hides inside an HTTP 200 Each fetch is three requests. The library loads the video’s watch page to read an API key, posts to YouTube’s internal player endpoint as the Android app, then downloads the caption track the player lists. From a datacenter IP the first request goes through: about 1.3 MB of HTML, key included, no captcha. The second also returns 200, but its body says LOGIN_REQUIRED , with the bot check as the reason. The library raises RequestBlocked and never sends the third. Both requests return 200; the second one’s body is the bot check. So curling youtube.com from your server proves nothing: the page loads and every status code is 200. Without a proxy config the library doesn’t retry, and retrying yourself from the same IP gets the same answer. IpBlocked is the other flavour: an HTTP 429, or a reCAPTCHA page where the watch page should be. It subclasses RequestBlocked , so one except RequestBlocked catches both. Versions before 1.0.0 reported the same block as TranscriptsDisabled (“Subtitles are disabled for this video”), so if an old pinned version swears a popular video has no subtitles, it’s probably being blocked too. A green smoke test can hide a blocked server On that blocked server, one video still worked: Rick Astley’s Never Gonna Give You Up, dQw4w9WgXcQ , the go-to test video. It came back all three times. Nine other popular videos raised RequestBlocked . A deploy check that fetches only that id goes green while the jobs behind it fail. Check a server with the videos your job needs. If most of them raise RequestBlocked , it’s the IP. Check your server · Python from youtube_transcript_api import YouTubeTranscriptApi api = YouTubeTranscriptApi () ids = [ # use your own " dQw4w9WgXcQ " , " kJQP7kiw5Fk " , " arj7oStGLkU " , ] for vid in ids : try : t = api . fetch ( vid ) print ( vid , " OK " , len ( t )) except Exception as e : print ( vid , type ( e ). __name__ ) # From a cloud server: # dQw4w9WgXcQ OK 61 # kJQP7kiw5Fk RequestBlocked # arj7oStGLkU RequestBlocked Cookies are off in 1.2.4, and proxies need upkeep The error message offers cookies as its second fix, with a warning that YouTube will eventually ban the account you log in with. In 1.2.4, the current release, cookie auth is switched off (“Cookie auth has been temporarily disabled”), CLI flag included. Its first fix is a proxy. The README recommends rotating residential proxies, because YouTube bans static ones after extended use. There’s a built-in config for one residential provider, and GenericProxyConfig for any other: Any proxy · adapted from the README from youtube_transcript_api import YouTubeTranscriptApi from youtube_transcript_api.proxies import GenericProxyConfig proxy = GenericProxyConfig ( http_url = " http://user:pass@my-custom-proxy.org:port " , https_url = " https://user:pass@my-custom-proxy.org:port " , ) ytt_api = YouTubeTranscriptApi ( proxy_config = proxy ) ytt_api . fetch ( video_id ) Know how retries behave before you buy traffic. The built-in provider config retries a blocked video up to 10 times; GenericProxyConfig tries once unless you subclass it and raise retries_when_blocked . Every attempt starts over at the watch page, so each refusal still costs a full page of traffic, and residential traffic is billed by the gigabyte. If the videos are your own, there’s an official route. The YouTube Data API’s captions.download needs OAuth and permission to edit the video, and each call costs 200 of your 10,000 daily quota units, so 50 downloads a day. It can’t read anyone else’s videos. Or take YouTube off your server: one GET With a hosted API, your server makes one HTTPS call and the YouTube side happens elsewhere, so it stops mattering where your code runs. LurkAPI’s transcript endpoint fetches the captions for you, and a cached repeat comes back in 20 ms. Same ten videos: 1 from the library, 10 from LurkAPI. Video transcript : What's said in a video or Short: its captions as timed segments and as one block of text. GET https://api.lurkapi.com/v1/youtube/video/transcript · 1 credit per call · Read the docs Get a transcript · 1 credit curl "https://api.lurkapi.com/v1/youtube/video/transcript?url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=arj7oStGLkU" \ -H "x-api-key: $LURK_KEY " The JSON, trimmed to 2 segments Response { "success" : true , "credits_charged" : 1 , "videoId" : "arj7oStGLkU" , "url" : "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=arj7oStGLkU" , "language" : "English" , "languageCode" : "en" , "isGenerated" : false , "transcript" : [ { "text" : "So in college," , "startMs" : 12645 , "endMs" : 14015 , "startTimeText" : "0:12" }, { "text" : "I was a government major," , "startMs" : 15349 , "endMs" : 16913 , "startTimeText" : "0:15" } ], "transcript_only_text" : "So in college, I was a government major, …" , "availableLanguages" : [ { "code" : "ar" , "name" : "Arabic" , "isGenerated" : false }, { "code" : "hy" , "name" : "Armenian" , "isGenerated" : false }, { "code" : "bg" , "name" : "Bulgarian" , "isGenerated" : false } ] } Each call is 1 credit: $0.45 to $0.90 per 1,000 transcripts depending on the pack , and a new account starts with 100 free credits. Switching from the library takes a few lines. Segments come back as text , startMs and endMs ; to_snippet converts one to the library’s text , start and duration : Python · 1 credit import requests API = ( " https://api.lurkapi.com " " /v1/youtube/video/transcript " ) KEY = " lk_live_... " def transcript ( video_id ): r = requests . get ( API , params = { " url " : video_id }, headers = { " x-api-key " : KEY }, timeout = 30 , ) r . raise_for_status () return r . json ()[ " transcript " ] def to_snippet ( seg ): s = seg [ " startMs " ] e = seg [ " endMs " ] return { " text " : seg [ " text " ], " start " : s / 1000 , " duration " : ( e - s ) / 1000 , } segs = transcript ( " arj7oStGLkU " ) print ( len ( segs ), to_snippet ( segs [ 0 ])) # 315 {'text': 'So in college,', # 'start': 12.645, 'duration': 1.37} One default differs. The library asks for English only and raises NoTranscriptFound otherwise; the endpoint returns English when the video has it and falls back to the video’s main language when it doesn’t. Pass language=es (or pt-BR , and so on) for a specific track, and check languageCode if you need English. A video with no captions returns 404 not_found . For a whole channel, list its uploads with channel videos and make one transcript call per video. For one transcript without code, the free YouTube transcript tool runs the same endpoint in your browser, or try it here: Run GET /v1/youtube/video/transcript in the live playground Questions What does RequestBlocked mean in youtube-transcript-api? YouTube answered the library’s player request with “Sign in to confirm you’re not a bot” instead of captions, almost always because the request came from a cloud or datacenter IP. IpBlocked, a subclass, means an HTTP 429 or a reCAPTCHA page; except RequestBlocked catches both. Why does youtube-transcript-api work locally but not on a server? Same code, different IP. YouTube blocks most IPs that belong to cloud providers such as AWS, Google Cloud and Azure, and a home IP can be blocked too after too many requests. Do cookies work with youtube-transcript-api? Not in 1.2.4. Cookie auth is switched off in the code, CLI flag included, even though the RequestBlocked message still suggests it. How do I use a proxy with youtube-transcript-api? Pass a proxy_config to YouTubeTranscriptApi: the built-in config for one residential provider, or GenericProxyConfig(http_url=..., https_url=...) for any other. The README recommends rotating residential proxies, since static ones get banned after extended use. Is there an official YouTube transcript API? Only for videos you can edit. The YouTube Data API’s captions.download needs OAuth and edit permission, and costs 200 of the default 10,000 daily quota units per call. For anyone else’s videos, LurkAPI’s transcript endpoint returns the captions for 1 credit a call.

title: How I Overhauled DocsGPT's Ingestion Engine & Supercharged RAG Context: My Hacktoberfest 2026 Journey
author: Sudhir Sharma
summary: How I Overhauled DocsGPT's Ingestion Engine & Supercharged RAG Context: My Hacktoberfest 2026 Journey Hacktoberfest is often seen as a sprint to collect 4 quick pull requests. But this year, I wanted to do something different: dive head-first into one of the most prominent open-source AI knowledge bases—DocsGPT —and tackle real, hard distributed systems and RAG optimization challenges that make a difference for thousands of production deployments. Over the course of October, that mission turned into 3 major pull requests, thousands of lines of robust Python and TypeScript, a deep dive into Celery, Redis, and pgvector, and an incredible journey collaborating with DocsGPT maintainer Alex (@dartpain) and @coderabbitai. Here is the deep-dive story of how I found the bugs, the architecture behind the fixes, how our ingestion overhaul (PR #3252) got merged into main, and what I learned along the way. The Mystery of the 24-Hour Source Lockout (PR #3068) The Sighting It started with an issue report that sounded almost impossible: “When I add or remove files rapidly in a source, DocsGPT locks me out of my source for 24 hours!” If you've ever worked on a document portal, you know that users don't wait patiently. They upload a PDF, realize they picked the wrong version, delete it, and re-upload. In DocsGPT, doing this triggered a phantom freeze. The UI spun indefinitely, and any attempt to re-sync returned deduplication errors. Root Cause Investigation Digging into the backend task dispatcher, I found the culprit in the Celery/Redis idempotency lock decorator. To prevent duplicate re-ingestion jobs, DocsGPT synthesized an idempotency key with a static 24-hour Time-To-Live (TTL). The architectural flaw: If a worker crashed, raised an uncaught network timeout to an embedding provider, or was terminated mid-task, the lock in Redis was never cleared. Worse, on the frontend, the Server-Sent Events (SSE) listener was waiting for an active task ID. When a duplicate task was deduplicated into a sentinel object, the frontend listener stayed in an infinite wait loop—a classic poison-loop. The Implementation Plan Dynamic Lease Expiration: Switched the static 24h key to a heartbeated lease with automatic release on terminal worker failure. Strict Task-ID Correlation: Updated FileTree and the SSE reingest pipelines to verify task ownership before blocking state transitions. Poison-Loop Recovery: Ensured that sentinel deduplication events explicitly notify the frontend state machine to release the UI spinner gracefully. Ingestion Resumption, Orphan Cleanup & Real-Time Queue Telemetry (PR #3252 — Merged! 🎉) While testing large docsets, another systemic bottleneck became obvious: long ingests. When ingesting massive documentation portals (thousands of pages from a sitemap or hundreds of markdown files from a GitHub repository), two critical failure modes occurred: The Worker Restart Death Sentence: If Celery was restarted (e.g., during a container redeploy or spot instance preemption) 90% of the way through a 2-hour ingest, the entire job was obliterated. All embedding tokens and compute spent were lost, forcing the user to start from scratch. Orphaned Vector Pollution: If an ingest failed without a linked source entity, thousands of embedding chunks remained stranded in PostgreSQL (pgvector), silently degrading vector similarity search precision. Designing the Solution Together with the DocsGPT team, I designed a multi-layer ingestion reliability overhaul across 16 commits: Database-Backed Checkpointing (0062_ingest_resume.py): Created a new IngestChunkProgress model and repository. As documents are parsed and vectorized in batches, chunk boundaries and offsets are recorded transactionally. Reconciler Auto-Resume: Built an automated recovery hook in docsgpt/parser/ingest_resume.py. On worker boot, any interrupted task is inspected, its vectorstore progress verified, and ingestion resumes from the exact un-embedded offset. Automatic Orphan Sweeper: Engineered a cleanup sweep in docsgpt/api/user/ingest_orphans.py that identifies unlinked vector embeddings in pgvector and purges them if an ingestion pipeline is aborted. Real-Time Queue Depth Gauge (events/queue_gauge.py): Built an SSE-streamed queue depth and head-of-line wait time gauge so users can see exactly where their documents stand in the worker queue. Result: Lead maintainer Alex (@dartpain) reviewed and merged PR #3252 directly into DocsGPT main! [Merged] fix(ingest): resume, dedup, size caps, orphan cleanup and queue gauge for long ingests #3252 dartpain merged 16 commits into main from fix/ingest-reliability SuperCompress: Extractive Boilerplate Pruning for RAG (PR #3247) With ingestion rock-solid, I tackled the next frontier in modern RAG: Context Window Efficiency (Issue #2578). The Problem: Token Bloat in Retrieval In enterprise RAG systems, retrieved documentation chunks are littered with noise: Breadcrumb trails: Home > Products > Developer Settings > v1 > API Cookie consent headers, footer links, and privacy disclaimers Repeated markdown table headers across adjacent chunks These lines consume 25% to 40% of the LLM prompt budget, pushing out real factual context and increasing inference latency and cost. The Engineering Challenge Naive regex or string stripping is dangerous in technical documentation: If a user asks "How do I configure the API?", stripping Home > Products > API might remove the very subject of their search. Stripping blank lines can break Markdown fenced code block syntax or remove four-space indentation on the first line of code. Numeric comparison operators (value > 10) look suspiciously like breadcrumb separators (>) and can be falsely pruned! The Architecture: CompressingRetriever I built an extractive boilerplate pruning stage in docsgpt/retriever/stages/boilerplate_pruning.py and wrapped it cleanly in CompressingRetriever inside dispatcher.py: python class CompressingRetriever(BaseRetriever): """Delegating retriever that applies post-retrieval boilerplate pruning.""" def init (self, inner: BaseRetriever): self._inner = inner def search(self, *args, **kwargs) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]: # Fall back to the inner retriever's stored question when search() receives no query if args: query = args[0] elif "query" in kwargs: query = kwargs["query"] else: query = ( getattr(self._inner, "original_question", None) or getattr(self._inner, "question", None) or "" ) docs = self._inner.search(*args, **kwargs) from docsgpt.retriever.stages.boilerplate_pruning import prune_boilerplate return prune_boilerplate(docs, query=query or "") Key features: Fenced-Code Preservation: Carries active_fence state across chunk boundaries so continuation chunks don't have their code lines stripped as navigation. Query-Aware Anchor Protection: Evaluates query terms before pruning; if a breadcrumb contains a user query term, it is protected. Mathematical & Table Guards: Preserves pipe tables, indented code, and signed comparison expressions (x > 5). The Human-AI Review Dynamic: Shoutout to @dartpain & @coderabbitai A huge part of why this Hacktoberfest was so rewarding was the review experience. Maintainer Appreciation: Alex (@dartpain) Maintaining a fast-moving, high-traffic repository like DocsGPT is demanding. Alex demonstrated what top-tier open-source stewardship looks like: prompt reviews, clear architectural expectations, and decisive merges when code met standards. His trust in letting me tackle deep parts of the ingestion engine was immensely motivating. The Relentless Precision of @coderabbitai DocsGPT employs CodeRabbit AI on every PR. At first, you might think an automated bot is just another linter. But CodeRabbit acted like an ultra-thorough senior engineer who never sleeps. It caught subtle, high-impact edge cases that would have taken days of production debugging to surface: Fenced-code continuation: Highlighting that continuation chunks inside a fenced code block without an opening fence could have unindented code mistakenly pruned. Leading indentation retention: Catching that .strip() on a joined string stripped leading indentation from a first-line code block. Stored question fallback: Pointing out that Dispatcher and ClassicRAG support search() using the question supplied at construction, meaning the wrapper needed to query self.original_question rather than passing an empty string. Each piece of feedback became an opportunity to write cleaner, more defensive Python and back it with comprehensive unit tests. Key Takeaways for Open Source Contributors Find Real Pain Points: Don't just fix typos. Dig into open issues where users are hitting actual walls (like failed 2-hour ingests or locked sources). Write Tests for the Edge Cases You Didn't Think Of: Automated reviewers and CI checks are your friends. Every time a reviewer points out an edge case, write a dedicated test for it. Respect Maintainer Time: Write clean PR descriptions, link related issues, ensure DCO sign-offs (git commit -s), and keep your branches rebased against main. Hacktoberfest 2026 has been an absolute blast. Huge thanks to the DocsGPT community, DigitalOcean, and MLH for organizing this global celebration of open source. See you on the leaderboard, and happy hacking! 🚀 Follow my open-source work on GitHub: @satanic47 Portfolio & Live Demos: shivysidinfo.tech

title: 111, 133, 172: The Same 192 Characters in Three Tokenizers
author: WGG
summary: I keep a bad habit: when a prompt looks short, I assume it is cheap. Then I pasted one Chinese code-review request into three tokenizers. Same 192 characters: 111 tokens in DeepSeek V4, 133 in o200k_base , 172 in cl100k_base . A 55% spread. The rule I had been using, four characters per token, predicts 48. The text asks for two failure modes of a Redis read-through cache in front of a Postgres analytics database, whether a 60-second TTL suits a financial reporting dashboard, and one metric to add before merging. The author expects p99 to fall from 1200 ms to under 50 ms at 12k requests per minute. 你是一名资深后端工程师，正在评审一个合并请求：在 PostgreSQL 分析库前面加一层 Redis 读穿缓存。 所有聚合查询的缓存时间都是 60 秒。作者预计看板接口的 p99 延迟会从 1200 毫秒降到 50 毫秒以下，高峰期每分钟 1.2 万次请求。 请列出两个风险最高的故障场景，判断 60 秒是否适合财务报表看板，并给出合并前应加的一项监控指标。每条不超过 80 字。 Where the count comes from Byte-level BPE does two things. A regular expression pre-splits the text into chunks: words with their leading space, runs of digits, punctuation, runs of whitespace. Each chunk then starts as individual bytes, and the tokenizer merges the highest-ranked adjacent pair until no listed pair remains. The merge list is learned, so frequent pairs rank high. That pre-tokenization step sets a hard boundary: merges never cross a chunk border, even when the vocabulary holds the pieces on both sides. Vocabulary size matters too. cl100k_base has 100,277 entries, o200k_base 200,019, DeepSeek V4 129,280, special tokens included. Text Characters o200k_base cl100k_base DeepSeek V4 What is a token in AI? 22 7 7 7 你好，世界！ 6 4 7 4 東京の天気は晴れ 8 7 10 7 什么是 AI 里的 token？ 16 7 10 6 Code-review sample 192 133 172 111 English barely moves: 7 tokens in all three for the 22-character question. Chinese and Japanese do. In cl100k_base the character 世 is not a token, so 你好，世界！ spends two byte tokens on it. 🦜 is 4 bytes in UTF-8 and 3 tokens in o200k_base — F0 9F , A6 , 9C — and none of those pieces is a character on its own. The full measured table, with the other samples, is in the tokenizer guide . Code is not prose either The four-character rule was calibrated on English prose, and code breaks it in a different direction. Punctuation, indentation and repeated short keys all cost tokens. Pretty-printed JSON carries spaces and newlines that minified JSON does not, and the minified text is what the API receives if you send it as a string. A 10,000-character file can need more tokens than the character estimate suggests. Claude and Gemini: estimates by design Claude and Gemini do not publish tokenizers for local use, so any local count for them is an estimate. Anthropic's count_tokens endpoint takes the same body as a message request, and its documentation calls the result an estimate. The docs also say Claude 4.7 and later produce about 30% more tokens for the same text than earlier Claude models. Google's models.countTokens does the same job for Gemini. GPT-6 is in the same position for a different reason: tiktoken 0.14.0 has no entry for it, and OpenAI has not published its tokenizer. A local tokenizer also measures one string. A request adds role markers, separators, a system prompt, tool definitions, images and files. OpenAI's /v1/responses/input_tokens counts a complete request for that reason. Estimate first, then measure With only a character count, English prose runs about 4 characters per token; Chinese is roughly 0.5 to 1.0 token per character, Japanese 0.6 to 1.0, Korean 0.5 to 1.0. For this sample the Chinese band is 111 to 172 tokens. Use the low end for a sanity check, the high end for a limit you must not cross. For o200k_base , cl100k_base and DeepSeek V4 the vocabularies are downloadable, and this counter reproduces the reference ids: import tiktoken enc = tiktoken . get_encoding ( " o200k_base " ) ids = enc . encode_ordinary ( " What is a token in AI? " ) print ( len ( ids ), ids ) # 7 [4827, 382, 261, 6602, 306, 20837, 30] Use encode_ordinary() for user text: plain encode() raises ValueError when the text contains <|endoftext|> . For DeepSeek, load the official tokenizer.json from the offline package with the tokenizers library. In the guide's test, the package's own demo used transformers , but 5.18.0 returned an empty list for Chinese text while 4.57.6 and tokenizers 0.23.2 returned the expected ids. Reading limits and prices A context window is a maximum; the input limit is the number to divide by. gpt-4o is 128,000 tokens, gpt-5.5 is 1,050,000, claude-opus-5-5 is 1,000,000, gemini-3.1-pro-preview is 1,048,576, and text-embedding-3-small is 8,192 per input. Text that fills the window leaves no room for the answer, and the request adds instructions and formatting on top. Prices are per million tokens, input and output separately: cost = input_tokens × input_price / 1,000,000 + output_tokens × output_price / 1,000,000 The 192-character sample plus 1,000 output tokens costs $0.030665 on gpt-5.5 at $5 input and $30 output per million, and $0.0012333 on deepseek-flash at peak rates of $0.30 and $1.20. Output dominates both. Above 272,000 input tokens, gpt-5.5 and GPT-6 price the whole request at 2× input and 1.5× output; Gemini moves above 200,000. The whole request moves, not just the excess. DeepSeek charges half its peak rate outside peak hours. What I changed Four characters per token remains fine for English sanity checks. For CJK text, code, JSON or tables, I count with the tokenizer that will run the request, add the system prompt and tool schemas, then leave room for the answer. The 48-token estimate was not off by a rounding error; it was less than half of every real count on this text.

title: I tested 748 crypto trading strategies and open-sourced the code and autopsy reports of the corpses
author: Manish Kumbham
summary: A few weeks ago I wrote hundreds of hypotheses for crypto trading strategies, re-screened every bot from my last post ( https://www.reddit.com/r/algotrading/s/dF5qfUNaCa ) and open-sourced the whole pile: 748 strategies in total with full code and report cards showing exactly where each one died and why. (That's 416 from last time plus 332 new corpses. The new ones are smarter strategies than before for the most part...) https://github.com/CacheCarti/Crypto-Strategies The pipeline runs 7 stages on real Binance data: code safety, in-sample, OOS, rolling walk forward, randomized starts, slippage stress and a holdout slice that nothing touches. Ran it on cloud VMs this time instead of my dying laptop, so the screening could actually get stricter. What the new pipeline found: Re-ran the 416 bots from my last post. 0 of 416 re-passed in the strictest config, including all 10 of my "survivors". Most die at out-of-sample with negative OOS (-85 to -900bps). The best one, rel_strength_eth_v3, made it to stage 5 and died at holdout. So my "validated" bots were mostly my old screening being sloppy and luck :) In the second config (slightly more lenient) exactly 1 of 416 re-passed, and it was a bot I had originally rejected (weekend_season_eth_v6, +325bps OOS). My graveyard had the only bot that actually lived. The 332 new corpses came from 559 hand-written bots (mixed with another batch, messy to release all at once). 384 screened, 332 dead (published), 52 survived and stay private for further testing. (Yes yes I know 52 is stupidly high, there's a reason for this at the bottom!) Admits per batch: v2 5/42, v3d 0/26, v3h 0/96, v4 3/92, v5 17/52, v6 18/60, v6b 9/16. v3h went 0 for 96, which tracks, it was basically like a monkey typing random keys, just a sweep of untested ideas. v5-v6b were narrow parameter neighbors of a mechanism that already worked. Please don't read the admit rates as some kind of quality check for the batches!! Why the rebuild?: The comments on the last post were right about my sloppy methodology (it still admittedly is sloppy here, but it got better later). It's also built on Google VMs now so I can create a new batch and test faster. I'll drop the batches weekly: Stricter judge: higher OOS thresholds, enforced holdout and a dev/holdout split inside the window so one lucky slice can't pass Every report card shows the exact gate that killed the bot, so you can figure out how to improve it Every batch is hashed so you can check when it was judged and by what I later added a 6+ year certification and a combined replay on 2.75 years, with DSR, PBO, plateau, regime splits, trial-ledger correction. Those results are still being evaluated, they'll come later. One disclosure about report cards vs actual performance: I cross-checked some strategies against QuantConnect classics this week and it surfaced a bug I didn't notice. Some bots emit a "flat" signal and my screen sometimes treated it as "hold". Impact is mostly ±100-300bps per strategy, around 25% of bots may fluctuate by that amount. The later stages and live paths honored flat completely. Yeah so I found a bug in my own judge while checking it against someone else's judge. The judge judges all, including the judge. If anyone improves the strategies and gets different results I'd love to see it. Happy to add tests people think are missing. Every suggestion so far has killed more of my bots... title: Where should a small studio launch its next Android app? A data experiment on 9,644 Google Play apps
author: Diogo Oliveira
summary: A market report for My MobApp Studio, written up as a scientific experiment. Code: Jupyter notebook my_mobapp_studio.ipynb . 1. The question Our studio has decided to build a new mobile app and launch it first on the Google Play Store. Before design starts, management asked four questions: How big is the market, in downloads and in dollars? How is that split across categories (as percentages)? Per category, how many downloads does a typical app get? Anything else that helps us pick the right bet. 2. Hypotheses Before touching the data, we wrote down what we expected to find, so the data could prove us wrong: H1. Games are the largest category by downloads. H2. Paid apps are a small share of downloads; the market is mostly free. H3. The more an app costs, the fewer installs it gets. H4. The Family category is the most valuable place for a paid app. 3. Data We used the public Google Play Store Apps dataset on Kaggle: 10,841 rows and 13 columns (App, Category, Rating, Reviews, Size, Installs, Type, Price, Content Rating, Genres, Last Updated, Current Ver, Android Ver). The newest "Last Updated" date is August 2018, so this is a snapshot of the store at that time, not today's market. Two properties of the data shape every number below: Installs is a bucket, not a count. "10,000+" means at least 10,000. We use the lower bound, so all download and revenue figures are minimums. There is no revenue column. We estimate revenue as Price x Installs for paid apps. Ads, in-app purchases and subscriptions are invisible, so this measures paid downloads only. 4. Method, step by step Step 1. Load and summarise. load_dataset() reads the CSV and print_summarize_dataset() prints shape, column types, descriptive statistics and missing values. Almost every column was loaded as text, Rating had 1,474 missing values, and one row was clearly shifted (its category was "1.9"). Step 2. Clean. clean_dataset() : dropped rows whose category is not one of the 33 real categories (removes the corrupted row); converted Reviews , Installs (strip "," and "+"), Price (strip "$") and Size (MB, with "k" converted and "Varies with device" set to missing) to numbers; removed duplicate apps, keeping the copy with the most reviews (the scrape listed many apps more than once); removed apps with 0 installs. This left 9,644 unique apps . Step 3. Explore. print_histograms() showed that installs, reviews and price are extremely skewed (a few giants, a long tail), so we plot them on a log scale. Ratings cluster around 4.3. compute_correlations_matrix() uses Spearman correlation because the data is skewed. Installs and reviews are almost the same signal (0.97), size has a mild positive link with installs (0.31), and price has a weak negative link with installs (-0.23). print_scatter_matrix() confirmed these shapes visually. Step 4. Answer the questions with group-by aggregations per category and the plots below. 5. Results 5.1 Market size Metric Value (lower bound) Apps analysed 9,644 Total downloads 75.3 billion Free apps 92.3% of apps, 99.92% of downloads Paid apps 744 apps, 57.4 million downloads Estimated paid-download revenue $291 million ...excluding novelty apps priced $100 or more $205 million One app, Minecraft ($6.99, 10M+ installs), accounts for about $70 million, or 24% of all estimated paid revenue. H2 is confirmed, more strongly than expected: paid apps are 7.7% of apps but less than 0.1% of downloads. 5.2 Downloads per category Category Installs % of total GAME 13.4 B 17.9% COMMUNICATION 11.0 B 14.7% TOOLS 8.1 B 10.8% FAMILY 6.2 B 8.3% PRODUCTIVITY 5.8 B 7.7% SOCIAL 5.5 B 7.3% PHOTOGRAPHY 4.7 B 6.2% VIDEO_PLAYERS 3.9 B 5.2% Other 25 categories 16.6 B 22.1% The full 33-category table is printed in the notebook. H1 is confirmed: Game is the largest category with 17.9% of all downloads, and the top 8 categories hold 78% of the market. Money is distributed very differently from downloads. Family takes 39.7% of estimated paid revenue , Lifestyle 19.8%, Game 14.0% and Finance 8.8%. Lifestyle and Finance are high only because of the "I am rich" novelty apps priced at $399.99. 5.3 Downloads per app, by category Total downloads reward crowded categories. To see what a single app can expect, we look at the median installs per app (the mean is distorted by giants like WhatsApp or Facebook). 1,000,000 median installs: Game, Photography, Video Players, Entertainment, Shopping, Weather, Education. 100,000: Communication, Productivity, Social, Travel, Health & Fitness, Sports, Maps, and others. 50,000: Tools, Family, News, Beauty. 1,000: Business, Medical, Events. Family is the most crowded category (1,873 apps, 19.4% of all apps) but a typical Family app gets only 50,000 installs. 5.4 Paid Family apps The top paid Family apps are all games: Minecraft (10M+), then Bloons TD 5, Where's My Water?, Card Wars, Cut the Rope GOLD and Infinity Dungeon VIP (1M+ each). Most cost between $0.99 and $2.99, and all come from established studios or brands. By installs, Arcade holds 47.8% of paid Family downloads, followed by Puzzle (14.6%), Role Playing (9.9%) and Strategy (9.4%). Arcade's share is driven mostly by Minecraft. H4 is partly confirmed: Family is where paid revenue concentrates, but most of it comes from one blockbuster. Without Minecraft, Family's estimated paid revenue drops from $116M to about $46M. 5.5 Prices In categories with at least 10 paid apps, the median price is low: between $1.49 and $5.04 everywhere except Finance. Finance ($165 mean vs $18.99 median) and Lifestyle ($109 vs $4.99) have inflated means caused by the $399.99 novelty apps. The most expensive app in each category is listed in the notebook; the top three ("I'm Rich - Trump Edition", "most expensive app (H)", "I Am Rich Premium") are all novelty apps. H3 is not supported within paid apps. Across all apps, price and installs are weakly negatively correlated (-0.23). Among paid apps, the median installs by price band are: up to $1: 500, $1 to $3: 1,000, $3 to $5: 5,000, $5 to $10: 1,000, over $10: 1,000. Being paid matters far more than the exact price: free apps have a median of 100,000 installs vs 1,000 for paid ones, with the same median rating (4.3 vs 4.4). 5.6 Additional insight: where competition is lighter We divided each category's median installs per app by its number of apps, a rough "demand per competitor" score. The top categories: Category Apps Median installs per app Weather 79 1,000,000 Entertainment 87 1,000,000 Education 106 1,000,000 House & Home 73 500,000 Video Players 164 1,000,000 These categories have few apps but a typical app still reaches about a million installs. 6. Conclusion Hypothesis Result H1. Games are the largest category Confirmed (17.9% of downloads) H2. The market is mostly free Confirmed (99.92% of downloads are free apps) H3. Higher price, fewer installs Not supported among paid apps; free vs paid is what matters H4. Family is best for a paid app Partly: 40% of paid revenue, but mostly one blockbuster Recommendation for My MobApp Studio: Launch free. Paid apps get roughly 100 times fewer installs for the same rating. Monetise with ads or in-app purchases, not an upfront price. Two candidate directions: a casual Game (Arcade or Puzzle), the biggest category with a 1M median per app, fitting our in-house game design team, but also the most competitive; a less crowded category such as Education, Entertainment or Weather, where few apps compete and a typical app still reaches about 1M installs. Avoid Family as a paid newcomer (crowded, low median, revenue concentrated in big brands) and Business, Medical and Events (median of 1,000 installs). 7. Limitations The data is a 2018 snapshot; the store has changed since then. Installs are lower bounds of buckets, so all figures are minimums. Revenue covers paid downloads only; in-app purchases and ads, the main revenue sources on Android, are missing. Duplicates were resolved by keeping the version with most reviews, which is a reasonable but not perfect rule. 8. What to experiment next Get fresher data , by scraping current Google Play listings, to check whether these patterns still hold. Bring in in-app purchase and ad revenue , using a "contains ads / in-app purchases" field from a newer dataset, to measure real monetisation rather than paid downloads. Model install success: train a simple model on category, genre, size, content rating and update frequency to predict which install bucket an app reaches. Analyse review text in the shortlisted categories to find what users complain about, which points to the gap our app should fill.

title: The health check passed while every job failed
author: Manh Liem
summary: I ran a paid red-team endpoint. The buyer page loaded, the form submitted, the job id came back 202 running, and the poll returned status: error every single time. The error read model endpoint unreachable at http://127.0.0.1:10100/v1 . The model was not unreachable. The health check was asking the wrong question. What the probe did The worker's first action before running any probe was a liveness check on GET /v1/models. That route belonged to a local model proxy that also serves a hosted provider roster. Building that roster required a refresh token for a third-party account. That token had expired, so the roster endpoint answered 500 Internal Server Error. The liveness check treated any non-200 as model unreachable and returned before running a single probe. The route that actually does the work is a different one: POST /v1/chat/completions. That route is served by a provider router, not by the roster. It answered 200 with a real completion the whole time. I confirmed this by sending one request with max_tokens: 1 and reading the response body. So the system had a working inference path, a broken metadata path, and a gate that checked the metadata path. Every job failed at the gate. Why this is worse than a hard outage A hard outage is visible. A gate that fails on a healthy system is silent and self-consistent. The buyer page returned 200, which is true. The submit endpoint returned 202 running, which is true. The job status said error, which was true. The liveness check said 500, which was false. Every individual response was accurate. The composition was not. Nothing in the logs contradicted the other lines, so the failure produced no anomaly to alert on. The check that would have caught it Run the same call the product runs, at the smallest size that still proves the path: POST /v1/chat/completions with a single token. One token costs almost nothing and exercises the exact route the product depends on. A metadata endpoint can be down, renamed, rate limited, or gated behind an expired token without affecting a single real request. Probing it tells you about the roster, not about your product. The second gate After fixing the probe, I added a monitor that runs one real job end to end every two hours and requires status done plus a non-empty report. That is the only check that covers the whole chain: page serving, submit, queue, worker, model call, and report write. Any single component can be healthy while the chain is broken, and a chain check is the only one that sees it. The cost is one real job per two hours. The alternative cost was a full day of traffic to a page where every submission failed.

title: The health check returned 200 while every buyer submission failed
author: Manh Liem
summary: A buyer page returned 200. A health check read that status, declared the service healthy, and reported success every five minutes for a full evening. In the same window, every submission from that page failed. The page was served by a CDN edge. The submission went to an origin tunnel that had died hours earlier. Two different things behind one status code A GET to a cached HTML page and a POST to a JSON API travel different paths. The CDN can answer the GET from cache with the last good copy, long after the origin stopped responding. The POST has no cache to fall back on, so it reaches the origin and returns whatever the origin returns. When the origin is a dead tunnel, the edge returns a 1033 error page. So the same hostname answered 200 to the check and an error page to the buyer. Both responses were accurate about their own request. The check measured the wrong request. Why the shortcut got added An earlier incident had the reverse shape. The origin was dead and the health check was probing a path that the edge answered statically, so the check said healthy while the buyer page was down. The fix was to probe the buyer page instead, because it depends on the origin. That fix was correct about which path to probe and wrong about which method to use. A cached GET does not prove the origin is up. The check improved and stayed broken at the same time. The check that actually proves it A POST that the origin has to answer with a specific value. In this case, a JSON-RPC tools list that must contain a named tool. That request cannot be satisfied from cache, cannot be satisfied by the edge, and cannot be satisfied by a dead tunnel. Either the origin answered with the expected content or it did not. One POST every five minutes costs nothing and covers the exact path a buyer takes. A GET to the same page would have cost the same and proved nothing. The general rule A status code is evidence about one request, not about a service. When a health check is written, the question to ask is not "does this endpoint return 200" but "is this the same request a customer makes". If the customer sends a POST with a body and the check sends a GET, the check is measuring a different system. Caches make this failure mode quiet. A dead origin produces a cached 200 that looks exactly like a healthy one, and every log line agrees with it. There is no anomaly to alert on until someone reads the buyer's error page. The cost of getting it wrong Five real submissions arrived from three separate networks. Every one of them failed at the origin. The health check reported success throughout, so nothing escalated. The traffic was real, the demand was real, and the product was down. The fix took one line. Finding it required reading the buyer's request instead of the checker's response.

title: One Domain, Different Answers: Reading Cloudflare and Google DoH JSON
author: WGG
summary: A colleague says a site loads on one network and fails on another. dig +short on your machine returns one address; a public resolver returns another. The same happens between two public resolvers: they can return different address sets for one name, and the JSON shows which mechanism produced the difference. The numbers below were measured on 2026-09-30 and 2026-11-03 with the ZeroTool DNS Lookup ; each applies to that date and those inputs. Both endpoints speak the same schema Cloudflare and Google expose a JSON profile of DNS over HTTPS: a GET with ?name= and ?type= . The binary form is RFC 8484; the JSON profile has no RFC. Cloudflare's documentation says it follows Google's schema, so the field names line up: Status (the RCODE), AD , Answer , Comment for resolver diagnostics. Google adds extended_dns_errors . The JSON profile works from a page because a cross-origin GET is enough. On 2026-11-03 both endpoints returned access-control-allow-origin: * . The tool sends Accept: application/dns-json , a CORS-safelisted header, so no preflight. A POST with a custom Content-Type triggers one. ECS explains most of the A-record differences Google Public DNS normally sends approximate network information to authoritative servers, usually zeroing out the last part of the IPv4 address. edns_client_subnet=0.0.0.0/0 disables that. Cloudflare's FAQ says 1.1.1.1 does not send ECS. A CDN that answers per subnet therefore hands the two resolvers different addresses. For www.qq.com on 2026-09-30: edns_client_subnet Google answer 114.114.114.0/24 121.14.77.201 , 121.14.77.221 8.8.8.0/24 43.159.109.55 139.130.4.0/24 43.168.224.173 Cloudflare ignored the same parameter and returned 43.159.109.55 , matching Google's 8.8.8.0/24 answer in that run. That is one name on one day, not a rule. Comparing resolvers means comparing vantage points: Google's answer moves with the subnet you name, Cloudflare's does not. do=1, and why AD is unreliable without it AD (Authenticated Data) reports DNSSEC validation. RFC 4035 §3.2.3 defines when it may be set; RFC 6840 §5.8 says a resolver should set it only when the query carried the DO or AD bit. Without do=1 the flag varies. On 2026-09-30, 30 queries per type for example.com : A, AAAA and NS returned "AD": false every time, MX returned true every time. With do=1 , and from Google either way, every answer had true . Send do=1 if you intend to read AD . Both resolvers then include RRSIG records in Answer , and the RDATA text is not byte-identical: on 2026-11-03 Google lowercased the covered type mnemonic, Cloudflare uppercased it. Compare sets, not strings. SERVFAIL is not a diagnosis. EDE is. A broken chain returns SERVFAIL and AD: false . SERVFAIL alone does not separate "DNSSEC validation failed" from "authoritative servers unreachable". The Extended DNS Error option (RFC 8914) carries a code plus text. For DNSSEC the relevant codes are 1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 12. dnssec-failed.org , 2026-11-03: Cloudflare: Status: 2 , Comment: ["EDE(9): DNSKEY Missing no SEP matching the DS found for dnssec-failed.org."] Google: Status: 2 , a Comment beginning "DNSSEC validation failure", and extended_dns_errors: [{ "info_code": 9, "extra_text": "No DNSKEY matches DS RRs of dnssec-failed.org" }] Code 9 is "DNSKEY Missing" (RFC 8914 §4.10). Cloudflare puts EDE(n): text strings in an array; Google puts a sentence in Comment and the code in extended_dns_errors . Parse the code, not the sentence. Google also adds Comment: "Response from <IP>." on an uncached answer. The same TXT record, 425 and 420 characters TXT values are sequences of character-strings, each at most 255 bytes (RFC 1035 §3.3). A long DKIM key is stored as several strings, and consumers join them with nothing between (RFC 6376 §3.6.2.2). In the 2026-11-03 query, Cloudflare returned each string quoted and space-separated; Google returned one unquoted string. For cf2024-1._domainkey.zerotool.dev , Cloudflare returned 425 characters with one " " join after the first 255-character string, Google 420. The gap is four quote characters plus the joining space. Google's documentation shows quoted, segmented TXT examples, so treat quoting as presentation, not a contract. Strip quotes when present, and never insert a separator between segments. A public resolver is not the system resolver dig asks the resolver configured in the OS, or the server you name. A DoH call asks Cloudflare or Google: different cache, different network position. /etc/hosts and VPN overrides: application lookups go through them; dig and nslookup normally do not read the hosts file, and a public DoH resolver sees neither. Split-horizon: internal names return internal addresses inside the network and NXDOMAIN outside. Search domains: the OS may append a suffix to a bare hostname; the JSON endpoints need the full name. Browser Secure DNS changes which resolver answers navigation, not the resolver the DoH request asks. Bootstrap: the page must resolve cloudflare-dns.com or dns.google first, so a filter that blocks them stops the lookup. Six misdiagnoses "Still propagating." Usually caching. Check the TTL, then ask a second resolver; old on one and new on the other means cache expiry. "DNS is broken on one machine." Check for a cached NXDOMAIN. RFC 2308 §5 lets a resolver cache the negative answer for the SOA minimum, so a fixed zone keeps failing until the timer expires. "The CNAME is missing." The resolver followed it and returned A/AAAA, or the apex uses CNAME flattening. Read the name field of each answer. "The TXT record is truncated." It is multiple 255-byte strings. Join them without a separator. "The internal name does not resolve." A split-horizon zone answers inside the network and returns NXDOMAIN outside. "DNSSEC is fine because the site loads." A validating resolver can fail where a non-validating one succeeds. NXDOMAIN and NODATA differ. Status: 3 means the name does not exist; NOERROR with zero answers means the name exists without that type. Reproduce it const url = `https://cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query?name= ${ encodeURIComponent ( ' zerotool.dev ' )} &type=MX&do=1&cd=0` ; const res = await fetch ( url , { headers : { accept : ' application/dns-json ' } }); const json = await res . json (); console . log ( json . Answer ); // [{ name, type, TTL, data }, ...] Swap the host to https://dns.google/resolve?name=…&type=…&do=1&cd=0 and add edns_client_subnet to see the ECS effect. Add AbortSignal.timeout(5000) and a try/catch ; the tool cancels each query after 5 seconds. One HTTP detail matters: in the same 2026-11-03 query, Google's response carried cache-control: private, max-age=300 and Cloudflare's carried none. A repeat query can be served from a browser or intermediary cache for up to five minutes, which looks like a resolver that ignored your change. The longer write-up, including record types, CAA, PTR and SRV, is in the DoH lookup guide .

title: Você delegou o código. Está perdendo a capacidade de revisá-lo?
author: Alex Pimenta
summary: O alerta sobre "cognitive surrender" ganhou tração. O problema não é só aprovar uma resposta errada: é deixar de exercitar as habilidades necessárias para perceber o próximo erro. Addy Osmani publicou, em 3 de novembro, Critical thinking when agents do the work . O texto não pede menos agentes. Pede o contrário: quem já vive em fluxo agentic precisa colocar pensamento crítico de volta no dia, porque o padrão do sistema não faz isso por você. O argumento central é um espectro. No topo, cognitive offloading : você delega a tarefa e mantém a propriedade do resultado — ainda julga, ainda pode rejeitar. No meio, deferral : a saída do agente vira o seu próximo input sem ser tratada como hipótese. Na base, cognitive surrender : a saída do modelo se torna a sua opinião; não resta visão independente para comparar. O termo vem do trabalho de Steven Shaw e Gideon Nave (Wharton). Em experimentos com 1.372 participantes, a mera disponibilidade de uma IA foi suficiente para muitas pessoas "entregarem" o raciocínio; em trials em que a IA estava errada, a taxa de aceitação do erro ficou alta, e a confiança dos participantes subiu mesmo assim. O detalhe que interessa a quem revisa código de agente é outro. À medida que os modelos melhoram, a porcentagem de erros óbvios cai. O output chega bem escrito, em geral correto o bastante para não exigir um segundo olhar. O intervalo entre pergunta e resposta encolheu para segundos. O que sumiu não foi só o tempo de espera: sumiu o espaço em que a gente costumava formar hipótese, testar alternativa e calibrar o próprio julgamento. Sem esse exercício, a capacidade de perceber o próximo erro atrofia — mesmo que o processo formal ainda exija "aprovação humana". Osmani descreve o deslize como gradual. Você leu bem a resposta anterior, então só passa os olhos na seguinte. Depois só o esqueleto. Um dia alguém aponta uma linha e você não consegue explicar — nem com a ajuda do agente. É aí que a dívida de compreensão ( comprehension debt ) aparece: o código existe, o time não tem mais modelo mental local para raciocinar a partir dele. As práticas que ele lista são simples e concretas: formar uma hipótese antes de pedir ao agente; perguntar o que teria de ser verdade para aquela conclusão estar errada e testar; definir "pronto" como evidência (teste, medição), não como narrativa do modelo; ler o que o agente de fato executou antes de ler o resumo; para cada check verde, nomear uma coisa que o check não cobre. A regra de ouro que ele cita do time de review do Claude Code encaixa: se você não consegue dizer o que as checagens deixariam passar, peça review de verdade, não aprovação rápida. A distinção com o debate de "humano no loop" importa. Lá a questão era se a recomendação do agente inclinava a decisão daquela rodada. Aqui a questão é se o modo de trabalho está formando — ou erodindo — a competência que torna a aprovação futura útil. Time que só assina diff sem exercitar o julgamento termina com processo de review e sem revisor capaz de divergir com base. Para quem já roda vários agentes em paralelo, o ponto prático é medir se ainda existe um momento em que o humano forma opinião antes de ver a saída e se a definição de "feito" continua sendo evidência, não fluência do texto. Leia o artigo mais aprofundado, com exemplos e a análise de arquitetura completa. Autor da série de livros "Engenharia de Software Assistida por IA" (disponível na Amazon).
